newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Hands off Lenin's body, communists tell Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Hands off Lenin's body, communists tell Yeltsin.

text.p: Russia's communist-dominated parliament plans to debate an emotional call on Thursday to President Boris Yeltsin not to move the mummified corpse of Vladimir Lenin from its mausoleum on Red Square.

The State Duma lower house, whose tsarist predecessor was abolished by Lenin when he installed the dictatorship of the Communist party after the 1917 revolution, voted overwhelmingly on Wednesday to debate the non-binding resolution entitled "Prevent an Act of Vandalism!".
Emotions were stirred by a remark by Yeltsin last week about a possible referendum on the issue, although in 1990 he came out against evicting Lenin from Red Square.

The communist legislators who drafted the motion quoted Jesus Christ and the head of the Russian Orthodox Church at the time of Lenin's death in 1924 to back up their argument that re-interring the body would be tantamount to sacrilege.

"In a civilised society, it is accepted that historic memorials should be preserved and the burial sites of its leading figures not touched, that national shrines should be honoured," the resolution said.
Democrats say Lenin should be re-interred. Historians say Lenin himself wanted a modest burial in St. Petersburg.
The communists said forces around the president wanted to "re-write history" and "wipe from the national memory everything linked to the Soviet period, its relics, memorials and shrines".
They also invoked UNESCO, saying the mausoleum from which generations of Soviet leaders reviewed parades on Red Square was an integral part of the U.N.-protected Kremlin heritage site.
Lenin's successors virtually deified the founder of the Soviet state and placed him at the centre of a communist system of values that functioned as a quasi-religion for seven decades.

However, rarely if ever would Soviet communists explicitly have called the tomb a "shrine". Today's nationalistic communist party has reconciled itself with the Orthodox Church, whose priests and believers were persecuted in Soviet times.
Once visited by millions, Lenin's tomb is still open to the public but draws smaller crowds. Since January, it has been closed while embalmers give the mummy its regular maintenance.
